body:
Before prediction markets existed, about the only thing the Oscars provided was vanity, uneducated opinions, and a bunch of elitists praising terrible movies. Most rational people would do just about anything to avoid this ostentatious, never-ending, parade of self-congratulatory nonsense.
Now, however, there’s some incentive to tune in. Prediction markets have done what no man thought possible: they’ve made dumb awards shows 
interesting. 
How? We have the opportunity to profit off 
them.
 Glorious, isn’t it?
So let’s dive right in and hunt for value at the Oscars! 
BEST ACTOR
Forget the actual movies, there’s serious drama happening in the Oscars 2026: Best Actor Winner market over on Polymarket. Take a look at this sudden, massive flip-flop :
Timothée Chalamet had been cruising along as a steady favorite, hovering just below 80% up until March, when he suddenly plummeted about 46 percentage points. A few days later the lead had completely collapsed, with Chalamet sinking into the low 30 percent range. Michael B. Jordan surged from a measly 10% all the way up to 60%, opening up a massive lead. That gap has since shrunk, with traders seeing value in Chalamet’s plummet. At the time of publication, Jordan held a 57%-30% lead over Chalamet.
How could Chalamet hold such a big lead for weeks and months only to see it evaporate? Did he announce his love for President Trump or support for babies in the womb?
Many are pointing to the
 2026 Actor Awards
 (formerly 
The SAG Awards, I assume the name was changed because of all the plastic surgery
) in which Jordan upset Chalamet to win Best Actor for his dual roles as the Smokestack twins in 
Sinners.
 Playing two characters, let alone ones named “Smoke” and “Stack”, is so cringe-worthy it should be an automatic disqualification, but that’s not what happened. 
There’s a good case to make that Skinny Timmy has some value here. Less than 3% of SAG voters are also Oscar voters.  The SAG Award predicts the winner for Best Actor about 70% of the time, but that leaves Chalamet a window to squeeze through, and considering he weighs about 150 lbs, he can fit through almost any opening. 
A quick note on value.  The way I’m thinking about this market is that Chalamet has maybe a 55% chance of winning.  Basically slightly over a coin toss.  (He was a massive favorite earlier in the cycle, but he said something mean about ballet and opera in an interview, so the petty Oscar voters are believed to want to punish him.)  I am far from “sure” he’s going to win, but at 30%, there is value here. 
This is the fundamental math of the game, even if it is a bit of a migraine-inducer. We should expect to lose about half the time —that’s just the reality—but the trade-off is a 233% payout when we’re right.
Now, if that level of risk (especially when it’s tied to probably terrible movies) makes you want to hide under the covers, that’s perfectly okay. There are plenty of other opportunities in other markets. The key is finding the specific flavor of risk you can stomach without driving yourself completely insane.
Overall, Chalamet is being priced as an underdog when he may very well be a slight favorite. 
Verdict: Underdog Chalamet = SOLID VALUE
LONGSHOT ALERT
Circling back to the Best Actor category, we can’t ignore the amount of snobbery floating around among the members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. For many of them, a primary goal in life seems to be appearing just a little more cultured than the next person. One way they accomplish this is by elevating a major winner that most Americans have never heard of.
So if you’re looking for a longshot play, Wagner Moura for Best Actor is your guy. He’s an international darling, he gave a well-regarded performance, and most importantly, hardly anyone in America knows who he is. That combination checks a lot of boxes for Academy voters, who will no doubt feel very pleased with themselves as viewers are forced to stay up late listening to them praise a film no one saw and talk about an actor most have never heard of.  He’s sitting around 5%. It’s a long shot.
Verdict: Moura = LONGSHOT VALUE
BEST PICTURE
There are three certainties in life: death, taxes, and virtue signaling at the Oscars.

While we can’t know exactly how a group of adults whose job is watching other adults pretend to be different adults will vote on which of those adults pretended the best, there are a few clues that can point us in the right direction - and occasionally even toward a profitable one.
To find value, we have to think like the voters. The Academy isn’t the type of crowd that watches a movie and just enjoys it. They’re evaluating which film most successfully translates the Marxist musings of coastal elites into a two-hour lecture for everyone else. With that in mind, let’s take a look at the contenders:
The two movies at the top aren’t really competing on production quality or storytelling. They’re competing on two different left-wing tropes of the moment. 
Sinners
 centers on race and the familiar theme of white people exploiting black people through the so-called evils of capitalism, a message that reliably plays well in left-wing circles. 
One Battle After Another
, meanwhile, leans into something a bit more top of mind at Hollywood parties: the idea that the system itself, the country, the president, capitalism, needs to be torn down through a violent revolution.
If this were 2021, 
Sinners
 probably wins in a landslide. But in 2026, with paid protesters on street corners waving “No Kings” signs and chasing ICE agents around cities, the revolutionary vibe feels much more in fashion. I’m leaning 
Battle. 
At time of writing it’s at 77%. (That’s a return of about 30% on your money, not a bad weekend.)
Verdict: Battle = MODEST VALUE
Thanks for reading! This post is public so feel free to share it with your friends.

SEAN PENN
Sean Penn is sitting at around 72% for Best Supporting Actor. And no, that’s not for his role flying to Ukraine to chat with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, though he did deliver a convincing performance there as someone trying very hard to seem important while not actually being important.
Penn checks off a lot of Academy boxes, given his political activism. They might even vote for him just so he has a chance to mumble on stage for a few minutes. So, as much as it pains me to say it, Penn at near 70% appears to be decent value. That said, I’ll happily accept any comments explaining why he might lose below, if for no other reason than to give me hope that Sean Penn might suffer a humiliating defeat and be forced to go reclaim the Oscar he gave to Zelenskyy.  
I’ll probably stay away from this market, but I did want to make sure I was able to make a bunch of Sean Penn jokes.
Verdict: Sean Penn = UNCLEAR
